scope: every workspace member listed in the root Cargo.toml and its non-test Rust source — its src tree and its Cargo build script — excluding inline cfg(test) modules, files under a tests directory, and files named test*.rs; public API is resolved through the module tree and its re-exports, and driver types through each file's own use statements

decision.summary: DD-147 froze who may declare the driver and who may write SQL. Neither observes the capability underneath both: a crate that is handed a connection runs arbitrary SQL with no rusqlite token in its source, so condition 1 reports it clean and condition 2 counts only what it did once it had one. This ledger freezes the capability itself — who can obtain a connection, and which public API hands one out or requires the caller to already hold one.

threeFacts.yields: a public item whose return position names a driver connection type; this is the capability leaving the layer
threeFacts.demands: a public item whose parameter position names a driver type; a function that demands a connection forces its callers to acquire one, which is how an exempt crate below the layer can push the driver upward past it
threeFacts.holds: production source outside the layer that calls something classified as yields; the scanned names are derived from the yields set rather than listed, so a name that stops yielding a connection stops being looked for and a new one is looked for the moment it appears

decision.notStatedHere: who may declare the driver, and how much SQL each file holds. Both are DD-147's, in config/governance/persistence-dependency-ledger.json. A crate calling rusqlite::Connection::open directly must first declare the driver, and condition 1 fails on that.
decision.testOnlyDoor: Some consumers of a connection are tests that cannot sink into the layer: core's own tests build their fixtures from TestState and create_task_impl, which sit above it, and orchestrator-persistence/tests/round_trip.rs is a separate crate by Rust's design. They reach a connection through src/test_support.rs, compiled only under the `test-support` feature. The feature is not a hole the gate declines to look at: what the module exposes is inventoried in testOnlyYields and testOnlyDemands, fact 3 still scans production source for those names, and feature_edge_errors fails if any crate enables the feature from [dependencies] rather than [dev-dependencies]. Under resolver 2 a dev-dependency's features are not unified into a normal build, so `cargo build` cannot reach the module — verified by compiling a production caller and reading the E0433.

core.reason: sits above the layer since FR-130 Phase A moved the persistence code into crates/orchestrator-persistence. persistence-dependency-ledger.json still calls core the persistence layer, which was true when FR-136 wrote it and has not been true since Phase A; core's own driver residual is frozen separately in core-boundary-ledger.json

crates/daemon.reason: held no driver in production since FR-141 B2 moved its gRPC handlers' SQL into the layer. Its cfg(test) modules read the database back to assert on what those handlers wrote, so it declares the driver and the test-support feature under [dev-dependencies] only

crates/integration-tests.reason: declares the driver and the test-support feature under [dev-dependencies] and asserts against the database directly in tests/trigger_fire.rs, which is what makes it end-to-end evidence rather than a restatement of the layer's API. Marked forbidden rather than exempt so a production source file added to it would be caught

crates/orchestrator-persistence.reason: is the layer. Holding the driver here is the decision DD-147 recorded, not a residual. What this ledger governs about it is the opposite direction: what it hands out

crates/orchestrator-scheduler.reason: held no driver in production since FR-141 B3 moved its scheduling SQL into the layer, including create_dynamic_task_items, which had re-exported a &rusqlite::Connection through the scheduler's own public API. Its cfg(test) modules keep a [dev-dependencies] edge

crates/orchestrator-security.reason: core depends on orchestrator-security, not the reverse, so it cannot route through a layer above it, and it opens the orchestrator database by path with its own connection. The exemption covers holding a connection. It does not cover demanding one from its callers: eleven of its public functions take a &Connection, and the four open_conn calls in crates/daemon/src/server/secret.rs exist for no other reason than to build one for them. FR-141 closes that direction and leaves the holding direction exempt

crates/slack-gateway.reason: opens SLACK_GATEWAY_DB with no workspace dependencies at all. A different database is not this boundary; scanned by nothing here
